953.title: Who are we
953.hook: in British Punjab, Sikhs asked what made Sikhi distinct
953.howItsDone: Sikhs today still discuss what marks a Sikh, and the Sikh Rehat Maryada, the code of conduct, sets out the Sikh wedding around the Guru Granth Sahib with the Lavan hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mahant with the keys, and your line was shared things need care. What shared thing did you look after? Today, a question underneath all of this week's stories. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

A wedding is being planned in a Punjab village. The families are Sikh. Should the couple walk around a sacred fire, as their Hindu neighbors do and as their own grandparents did? Or around the Guru Granth Sahib, while the Lavan hymns are sung? An uncle says one thing, a cousin back from Lahore says another, and the bride's mother just wants everyone to stop shouting. A small family argument, about a very big question. Today: who are we.
screen: `A WEDDING BEING PLANNED.` → `AROUND THE FIRE, OR THE GURU?` → `A SMALL ARGUMENT, A BIG QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, a question at home. Without a Sikh kingdom, with missionaries preaching and reformers arguing, Sikhs found themselves asking something they'd once taken for granted: what actually makes a Sikh a Sikh? Second, the questions got very practical. Which wedding rite. Which names. Whether to keep the hair uncut. Whether caste customs belonged in the Guru's house. Some Sikhs had taken amrit, some kept uncut hair without it, some cut their hair and still called themselves followers of Guru Nanak. Third, two answers, both sincerely held. Some Sikhs saw Sikhi as living inside a wider Hindu world, sharing many festivals, customs and shrines with their neighbors, and saw no reason to draw sharp lines. Others argued that the Gurus had given the Sikhs their own scripture, their own rites and their own form, and that Sikhi stood on its own. Both sides loved the Gurus. They disagreed about what loving them required, and these lessons don't pick a winner. Fourth, the Gurus' own words. Guru Arjan, in a hymn in Raag Bhairo, says he is neither Hindu nor Muslim, and that his body and his breath belong to the One who is called both Allah and Ram. Sikhs on both sides of the argument read that hymn, and drew different things from it. The question didn't get one answer in a day. The next stretch of the story is the answers people built: societies, schools, books, a law about weddings. But it began with a family around a table, asking. That's today's word.
screen: `A QUESTION AT HOME.` · `WHICH WEDDING, WHICH NAMES, WHAT HAIR?` · `TWO ANSWERS, BOTH SINCERE.` · `NEITHER HINDU NOR MUSLIM.` · then, large: `WHO ARE WE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with your own question. Sit, and let your breath settle. Let one question rest in you for a while: what makes me me? Not your job title or your phone. Something deeper: a value you won't trade, a habit you keep even when nobody's watching, a place or a people you belong to. Let a few answers come and go. Notice which one stays. Hold it like you'd hold something fragile. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Who are we. The question Sikhs in British Punjab asked about weddings, names, hair and scripture, as they worked out what made Sikhi distinct. Today's word.
Your line: who are we. Today, ask someone you love what they think makes your family, or your circle, who it is. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

954.title: Bhai Maharaj Singh
954.hook: a Sikh saint who resisted the British was exiled and died in Singapore, where Sikhs remember him
954.howItsDone: Sikhs in Singapore keep a memorial to Bhai Maharaj Singh at a gurdwara there, and visitors come to pay their respects to him as a saint who resisted British rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a family table and a big question, and your line was who are we. What answer stayed with you? Today, one man who seemed very sure of his. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

Singapore, a busy port city far across the sea from Punjab. In a gurdwara there, the sangat keeps a memorial to a Sikh holy man from Punjab. He didn't come to Singapore to trade, or to serve in a regiment. He came as a prisoner, sent far away from Punjab on purpose. He never went home. But the people who remember him there have made sure he isn't forgotten. Today: Bhai Maharaj Singh.
screen: `A MEMORIAL IN SINGAPORE.` → `HE CAME AS A PRISONER.` → `HE NEVER WENT HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the saint. Bhai Maharaj Singh was a holy man in Punjab, the head of a dera, a religious center, where people came for his blessing and for langar. Bhai is a title of respect, meaning brother. People came to him for his devotion first; the resistance came later. Second, the resister. As the British took control of Punjab, he would not accept it. Sikh histories remember him moving through the countryside after the wars, encouraging resistance and refusing to surrender. The British saw him as dangerous: a respected holy man who could gather people around him. Third, the exile. When he was finally captured, the British didn't keep him in Punjab, where people might gather around him again. They sent him across the sea to Singapore and held him in prison there. Cut off from his people, his health failed, and he died in exile. Fourth, the line that fits him. In the saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur, near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says the wise one frightens no one and is afraid of no one. That is how Sikh tellings remember Bhai Maharaj Singh: not cruel, not afraid. And here's the turn in his story. He was sent away to be forgotten, and Singapore is where he is remembered. Sikhs there keep his memorial, and people still come to pay their respects. The far-off place his captors chose became the place that holds his name. That's today's word.
screen: `A HOLY MAN WITH A DERA.` · `HE WOULD NOT SURRENDER.` · `SENT ACROSS THE SEA TO SINGAPORE.` · `AFRAID OF NO ONE.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED FAR AWAY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a far-off grave. Sit, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone who is buried, or whose ashes rest, far from where you are: a grandparent in another country, a friend in another city, an ancestor whose grave you've never seen. If no one comes, think of all those who died far from home. Picture the place, as best you can. Say their name in your mind. Let them be remembered for these two minutes, right here. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Maharaj Singh. A Sikh holy man who resisted British rule in Punjab, was exiled to Singapore and died there, where Sikhs keep his memorial. Today's word.
Your line: remembered far away. Today, say the name of someone buried far from you, out loud or in a message to someone who knew them. Day nine hundred fifty-four.

955.title: Loss remembered
955.hook: Sikhs remember the annexation as the end of a kingdom and the start of a long question
955.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the fall of the Sikh kingdom in histories, songs and family stories, and the couplet raj karega khalsa is sung after the Ardas in gurdwaras, read by different Sikhs in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Maharaj Singh in Singapore, and your line was remembered far away. Whose name did you say? Today, how a whole people remembers what it lost. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

The Ardas has ended in a gurdwara, and the sangat is still on its feet. A few lines are sung together before everyone sits, and among them is a phrase: raj karega khalsa, the Khalsa shall rule. The throne at Lahore is long gone. The army that held at Chillianwala lost at Gujrat, the boy king was taken away, and the diamond went across the sea. And still the line is sung. What does it mean to sing of rule with no kingdom? Today: loss remembered.
screen: `THE ARDAS ENDS.` → `THE KHALSA SHALL RULE.` → `RULE, WITH NO KINGDOM?`

segments.voice: First, what ended. When Punjab was annexed after Gujrat, the kingdom Ranjit Singh had built was gone. No Sikh throne, no Sikh army of its own, a boy king sent to England. For Sikhs it is remembered as an ending. Second, how it was remembered. In stories, in histories, and in poetry. Shah Muhammad, a Muslim poet of Punjab, wrote a long Punjabi ballad of the first war between the Sikhs and the British, grieving the ruin of the Sikh army. Here the loss is mourned by a Muslim poet, in Punjabi words. Third, the long question. Without a kingdom, what is the Khalsa? Sikhs have given more than one answer, and they still discuss it. Take the couplet sung after the Ardas. Some Sikhs hear in raj karega khalsa a hope for Sikh self-rule on the earth. Others hear the rule of the Guru's way over one's own self, and point to the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat as what no army could take. These lessons don't settle it; they just tell you the question is alive. Fourth, the Guru's own way with loss. When Babur's armies came through Punjab, Guru Nanak did not look away. In a hymn in Raag Asa, he describes the suffering and asks God directly whether God did not feel the pain. Sikh scripture holds a lament like that: loss named out loud, before God. That is one way Sikhs remember. That's today's word.
screen: `THE KINGDOM ENDED.` · `A MUSLIM POET'S BALLAD OF THE WAR.` · `WITHOUT A KINGDOM, WHAT IS THE KHALSA?` · `GURU NANAK'S LAMENT.` · then, large: `THE LONG QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with an old loss. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind an old loss that came down to you from others: your family's, or your people's. A village left behind, a home sold, a language fading, a story nobody finished telling. Don't push it away, and don't dig into it either. Just sit beside it, the way you'd sit with someone who's grieving. Notice what question it still asks you. You don't have to answer it today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Loss remembered. How Sikhs remember the end of Ranjit Singh's kingdom: in stories, in poetry, in prayer, and in a question about the Khalsa that is still being asked. Today's word.
Your line: the long question. Today, write down one thing your family or community lost, and the question it still leaves you with. Day nine hundred fifty-five.

956.title: Loss and exile close
956.hook: a lost kingdom, a lost boy, a found faith
956.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the years after the fall of the Sikh kingdom as a time of loss and exile, and tell Duleep Singh's return to Sikhi as part of how the community found its footing again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, loss remembered, and your line was the long question. What loss did you write down? Today we close this whole stretch of the story, loss and exile. Day nine hundred fifty-six.

A great diamond, sent across the sea to a queen. It's the object at the center of one of these weeks' stories, the Koh-i-Noor, taken from a boy king and never given back. But there's an older jewel in this story, and nobody could put it in a box. Guru Nanak names it in the Japji: within the mind, he says, are jewels, gems and rubies, if a person listens to the Guru's teaching even once. A diamond can be taken. That jewel, the Japji says, is within. Today: loss and exile close.
screen: `A DIAMOND SENT ACROSS THE SEA.` → `AN OLDER JEWEL.` → `JEWELS WITHIN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: First, a kingdom lost. This stretch began with war with the British: Mudki and Ferozeshah, then Sobraon and a sense of betrayal, a treaty that gave away Kashmir, a queen sent away from her son. Then Multan rose, the army held at Chillianwala, lost at Gujrat, and Punjab was annexed. The kingdom ended. Second, a boy lost. Duleep Singh was raised by British guardians, baptized a Christian, settled in an English country house, far from Punjab. He met his mother again after long years apart, and she told him who he was. She died in London, and he carried her body toward home. Third, a faith found again. Stopped at Aden on his way to India, Duleep took amrit. He died in Paris, an exile. His daughters went on: Sophia marching for women's votes, Bamba keeping the family's memory in Lahore. Fourth, a people asking. Sikh soldiers served far away. Farmers moved to new canal land. Missionaries and reformers argued, mahants held the gurdwaras' keys, and families asked, who are we. Bhai Maharaj Singh, sent away to be forgotten, was remembered in Singapore. And the long question stayed open. So here's the shape of these weeks. So much was taken: land, army, throne, diamond, a boy's childhood. And yet the hymns, the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat were still there to come back to. Duleep came back. Sikhs kept asking. Next comes the answer people built: a stretch of the story called reform and renewal. That's today's word.
screen: `A KINGDOM LOST IN WAR.` · `A BOY LOST TO EXILE.` · `A FAITH FOUND AGAIN.` · `A PEOPLE STILL ASKING.` · then, large: `FOUND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for something found again. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you lost for a while and found again: a friendship, a faith, a habit, a part of yourself, a song, a place. Remember what it was like to be without it. Then remember the moment it came back, or the slow way it returned. Hold that return for a while. Let it be as quiet or as warm as it is. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Loss and exile close. The end of this stretch: a lost kingdom, a lost boy, and a faith found again. Today's word.

957.title: Baba Dayal
957.hook: a reformer in Rawalpindi taught worship of the formless God and simple Sikh ceremonies; his followers were called Nirankaris
957.tomorrow: Baba Ram Singh and the Namdharis
957.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember Baba Dayal of Rawalpindi as an early reformer who called people back to Nirankar, the formless God, and to simple ceremonies held before the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the story of loss and exile, and your line was found again. What did you find again? Today a new part of the long story opens: reform and renewal. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

A shopkeeper in Rawalpindi, in the north of the Punjab, keeps saying the same thing to anyone who stops by. God has no shape. God is not in the stone figure on the shelf, or in the ritual the priest charges for. God is Nirankar, without form, just as the Gurus sang. His name is Baba Dayal. He isn't raising an army or building a palace. He's asking people to strip their worship back to what the Gurus taught. The people who listened came to be called Nirankaris. Today: Nirankari.
screen: `A SHOPKEEPER IN RAWALPINDI.` → `GOD HAS NO SHAPE.` → `STRIP WORSHIP BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Nirankar is a name for God in the Guru Granth Sahib: the formless One, God without shape. In the Japji, Guru Nanak closes several verses by calling God the formless one who lives forever. Nirankari simply means a person devoted to that formless One. Second, what Baba Dayal saw. Histories of the period describe Sikh homes and shrines that kept images, costly rites, and Brahmin priests hired for births, weddings and deaths. Many Sikhs then saw no conflict in that. To Baba Dayal, it was drifting away from the Gurus. Third, what he taught. Remember the formless God and repeat the Name. Drop the images. Keep the ceremonies simple. His followers became known for weddings held before the Guru Granth Sahib, with the couple walking around the scripture as hymns are sung, the rite Sikhs call Anand Karaj. Some historians count Baba Dayal among the early reformers of the Sikh revival, and the Nirankaris kept his teaching alive in their own circle. Fourth, a name to keep straight. A much later group in Punjab also uses the word Nirankari in its name. It's a separate movement, and the two shouldn't be mixed up. When this lesson says Nirankari, it means Baba Dayal and those who followed him. Why it matters on an ordinary day: reform doesn't always start with a speech. Sometimes it starts with one person taking things away, the extra objects, the extra fees, the extra noise, until what's left is the thing that was meant to be there all along.

segments.voice: Two minutes of taking things away. Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one habit you do every day that has gathered extra steps over time: the morning scroll, the way you eat lunch, the way you pray or don't. Ask what the habit was for in the first place. Now picture doing it with one extra step gone. Just one. Breathe slowly while you look at the simpler version. If you pray, you can repeat Waheguru on each breath out, with nothing added. The bell holds the time.
Nirankari. One devoted to Nirankar, the formless God, and the name given to the followers of Baba Dayal of Rawalpindi. Today's word.
Your line: back to the formless. Today, simplify one habit. Take one extra step out of something you do, and see what's left. Day nine hundred fifty-seven.

958.title: Baba Ram Singh and the Namdharis
958.hook: a movement in white clothes, reciting the Name and boycotting British goods
958.howItsDone: Namdhari Sikhs wear white, tie their turbans straight across the forehead, recite the Name together, and remember Baba Ram Singh as a teacher of plain living and of refusing British goods and courts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nirankari, and your line was back to the formless. Which extra step did you take out of a habit? Today, a second reformer, with a firmer edge. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

White cloth. That's what you'd notice first. A crowd gathers in a village in the Punjab, and everyone is dressed in plain white, with turbans tied straight across the forehead. They're reciting the Name together. Some of them, caught up in it, cry out loud, and the neighbors start calling them Kukas, from those cries. Their leader asks them to do something bold for the time: don't use the British post, don't go to British courts, don't wear foreign cloth. The leader is Baba Ram Singh. Today: Namdhari.
screen: `A CROWD DRESSED IN WHITE.` → `RECITING THE NAME ALOUD.` → `NO BRITISH POST, COURTS OR CLOTH.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Namdhari is the name the movement chose for itself, and its followers understand it as one who holds the Name. Kuka was the neighbors' nickname, tied, the story goes, to the cries that rose up during their recitation. Second, the teacher. Baba Ram Singh came from the village of Bhaini, in the Ludhiana district, and he had served as a soldier before he turned to teaching. He called people to the Name, to the Khalsa's discipline, and to plain living: white clothes, no meat, no alcohol, honest work. He spoke against the dowry and against killing baby daughters, and he held simple weddings, sometimes for many couples at once, without heavy cost. Third, the refusal. Under British rule, Baba Ram Singh told his followers to stay away from British schools, courts, post and goods. Settle your disputes among yourselves. Weave your own cloth. Some historians see in this an early form of the boycotts of India's later freedom movement. The British watched him closely. Fourth, a fair word on difference. Namdharis hold that the line of living Gurus continued after Guru Gobind Singh, through Baba Balak Singh and Baba Ram Singh. The Akal Takht and the wider Khalsa Panth hold that Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib, and that no person holds it after him. This lesson tells his story, and leaves that question to each community. A simple rule, kept firmly, can say more than a long argument.

segments.voice: Two minutes in something plain. If you can, notice what you're wearing right now. Not to judge it. Just notice: the color, the weight, whether it's simple or busy. Namdhari. One who holds the Name; the followers of Baba Ram Singh, dressed in white, also nicknamed Kukas. Today's word.
Your line: simple and firm. Today, wear something simple, and keep one small promise to yourself without bending it. Day nine hundred fifty-eight.

959.title: Malerkotla, 1872
959.hook: Namdharis taken prisoner after a raid were executed by cannon on the order of British officials, without trial
959.howItsDone: Namdhari Sikhs gather at Malerkotla to remember the Namdharis executed there by cannon as martyrs, and the Sikh Ardas calls to mind those who kept their faith to the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Namdhari, and your line was simple and firm. Did you keep your small promise? Today ends a week that ran from who are we, through loss and found again, to two reformers. It ends hard. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.

This is a heavy day, so here is where it goes before it starts. Malerkotla is a small town in the Punjab, the seat of a princely state. Near it, Namdhari prisoners were tied to the mouths of cannon by order of a British official, and the guns were fired. There was no trial. Namdharis remember these men as shaheeds, martyrs, and they gather at Malerkotla to remember them still. Today isn't about the details of the killing. It's about how a community remembers. Today: Malerkotla.
screen: `A HEAVY DAY.` → `PRISONERS BEFORE THE CANNON.` → `NO TRIAL.` → `HOW A COMMUNITY REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: First, what led to it. Yesterday you met the Namdharis, with their white clothes and their firm refusals. Some of them were angered by the killing of cows, and a band of them attacked Malerkotla. There was fighting, and people of the town were killed as well as Namdharis. Namdhari histories say Baba Ram Singh had not sent them, and had tried to hold his followers back. Second, the response. The British official in charge of the district had the captured men brought out and executed by cannon, without a trial. A senior official approved more executions the next day. Even the British government found this too far, and the official was removed from his post. Third, a story Namdharis tell. Among the prisoners, they say, was a young boy. The official offered to spare him if he would deny his teacher. The boy refused, and was cut down. Treat this as the community's memory, told and retold, rather than a court record. Fourth, why it's remembered. The daily Ardas, the prayer Sikhs stand for, calls to mind those who gave their lives and kept their faith, and it ends by asking for the good of all, sarbat da bhala. Remembering, in that prayer, is not revenge. At Malerkotla, the town's own people were caught in the violence too, and this lesson keeps the same silence for their dead. That's the shape of today's line: saying the names, not letting them disappear, and not turning grief into a weapon.
screen: `A RAID, AND DEATHS ON BOTH SIDES.` · `EXECUTED BY CANNON, WITHOUT TRIAL.` · `A STORY NAMDHARIS TELL.` · `REMEMBERING, NOT REVENGE.` · then, large: `REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, and one of them in silence. For the first minute, breathe slowly and let the week settle: who are we, a loss remembered, something found again, two reformers. Then, for one full minute, keep silence for those who died at Malerkotla, the prisoners and the townspeople alike. No words needed. If you pray, you can stay with Waheguru in the quiet. If you don't, just hold the silence as a way of saying they mattered. The bell holds the time.
Malerkotla. The town in the Punjab where captured Namdharis were executed by cannon without trial, and where they're remembered as martyrs. Today's word.
Your line: remembered. Today, say one name of someone who's gone, out loud or in your head, and let it be enough. Day nine hundred fifty-nine.
